newsitem.title: GERMANY: Protesting German miners heed call to disperse.
newsitem.headline: Protesting German miners heed call to disperse.

text.p: Thousands of German coal miners protesting in Bonn against subsidy cuts began heading home on Tuesday, heeding an appeal from their union after Chancellor Kohl postponed crisis talks because of the threat of violence.

The miners had virtually besieged the government quarter since Monday to protest against cuts in government subsidies which they say will cost more than half of Germany's 90,000 pit workers their jobs.
Most of the 13,000 or so demonstrators began to disperse after a passionate appeal from the leader of the IG Bergbau miners' union, Hans Berger, who had been due to meet Kohl.
"Don't let them steal the arguments," he told a rally in the late afternoon. "Protest in your regions and if no compromise is reached, we are ready to come back!"

Kohl had said the talks could take place on Thursday, but only if the miners' protest ended. He told reporters he would not let himself be put under pressure but wanted the two sides to move towards each other in a reasonable fashion.
The miners' presence had created an unusually threatening atmosphere in normally sleepy Bonn, although violence was limited to isolated incidents.

By late afternoon, up to 8,000 miners were still on their way to Bonn from the coal mining region of Saar state, on the French border. Berger said he would hold another rally to explain the situation to these men and ask them, too, to go home and await the outcome of Thursday's talks.
Work stopped in Germany's 18 pits on Friday after Bonn said it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks by 2005 instead of the promised 6.5 billion, from over nine billion at present.
IG Bergbau says the government plans will force 10 pits to close by 2005, make 50,000 miners redundant and cause a further 70,000 related job losses in already depressed areas.
